title: Calibrate the mastery bar per skill
statement: A percentage mastery bar means something only while the task mix, difficulty and support stay fixed, so set it per skill, not by one global figure.
example: The reading course's feedback routing defines mastery through controlled evidence and downstream risk, not a global raw 90%.
detail: The assessment-as-signal BrainLift treats mastery as a decision rule applied to uncertain evidence: every rule trades a false promotion, which risks failure downstream, against a false non-promotion, which wastes time and motivation, and percent-correct only means something when task difficulty and evidence conditions are held steady. Its evidence base cites work showing mastery behaves more like a graded risk than a clean threshold, and the reading course's feedback routing defines mastery through controlled evidence and downstream risk, not a global raw 90%. Set the bar by weighing the cost of a false pass, advancing a learner too early, against a false fail.
against: The platform's rules for every app say to enforce mastery gates at 90% accuracy or more. A course-evaluation rubric in the same project enforces mastery gates at ≥90% accuracy (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/skills/timeback-course-eval/references/eval-criteria.md`, line 24).

a KC that many downstream units depend on (a Factor-2 root prerequisite in the load-bearing memo — camouflage, water cycle) gets a **conservative cut** because a false-pass compounds into unreadable later text; a terminal, low-transfer KC tolerates a looser cut because a false-pass costs little downstream.
the per-KC risk-tolerance table is the artifact this section commits to producing

- **Mastery boundary:** No global percentage, including 90 percent, is a course-wide mastery definition without task mix, independence, dependency risk, false-promotion cost, and downstream-use evidence.
The proposal rejects a global 90-percent mastery rule and requires controlled evidence, independence, risk, and downstream-use boundaries.
